issues.legal_issue: A statutory claim for tax recoverable as a public demand may take priority over a previously created mortgage when legislation expressly gives that claim precedence over mortgage debts.
material_facts: The bank held a mortgage over property belonging to the firm’s partners, created before the State sought to attach and sell the property for the firm’s sales-tax arrears.

The sales-tax legislation allowed the arrears to be recovered as an arrear of land revenue, and the land-revenue legislation gave claims recoverable under its recovery chapter precedence over other claims, expressly including mortgage claims.
issues.conclusion: The State’s claim for the sales-tax arrears had statutory priority over the bank’s secured mortgage claim.
issues.legal_principle: The common-law priority of Crown debts does not, by itself, extend over a mortgagee or other secured creditor; it ordinarily applies against unsecured creditors. A statute may expressly extend the State’s priority to secured debts. Under sections 13(3)(a) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957, and 190(c) and 158(1) of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964, the tax arrears were recoverable under the land-revenue recovery provisions and had precedence over mortgage claims. The Court relied on M/s Builders Supply Corporation v. Union of India, Collector of Aurangabad v. Central Bank of India, Bank of Bihar v. State of Bihar, and Giles v. Grover.

predicates.tax_priority_dispute_in_secured_creditor: A secured creditor and a public authority asserted competing claims to property in a dispute about priority for a tax debt.
predicates.tax_debt_recoverable_through_public_dema: The governing law allowed the tax debt to be recovered through a procedure for collecting public demands.
predicates.law_expressly_prioritizes_that_demand_ov: The governing law expressly gave demands recoverable through that procedure precedence over mortgage claims.

issues.definition: When a secured-creditor priority dispute concerns a tax debt recoverable through a public-demand procedure, and the law expressly prioritizes that demand over mortgages, the public authority’s tax claim takes priority over the mortgage debt.

issues.legal_issue: Partners may be held personally and jointly and severally liable for a firm’s tax debt, and their property may be proceeded against, when a specific statutory provision imposes that liability.
material_facts: The sales tax was assessed against the partnership firm, which the sales-tax legislation treated as a dealer and a person for assessment purposes.
The property sought to be proceeded against belonged to the firm’s partners.
A statutory amendment expressly made the firm and each partner jointly and severally liable for the firm’s tax, penalty, and other amounts due.
The bank’s decree remained unexecuted when the amended provision was in force.
issues.conclusion: The partners and their property were liable for the firm’s outstanding sales-tax dues under the specific statutory provision, notwithstanding that the assessment was against the firm.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25 of the Partnership Act, 1932, makes partners jointly and severally liable for acts of the firm, but the firm may be treated as a separate legal entity for the limited purpose of tax assessment, so that section 25 alone does not make partners liable for tax assessed against the firm. A specific statutory provision can impose that liability. Section 15(2-A) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957, did so. The Court relied on Commissioner of Sales Tax, M.P. v. Radhakrishan, which recognized the need for a specific provision, and Third Income-tax Officer v. Arunagiri Chettiar, which considered an express provision imposing partners’ joint and several liability.

predicates.firm_tax_assessment_dispute: A public authority sought to recover tax assessed against a partnership from the partners or their property.
predicates.tax_assessed_against_partnership_as_a_se: The firm was assessed as the relevant entity for the tax, rather than the partners being assessed individually.
predicates.specific_law_makes_partners_jointly_and_: A specific legal provision made each partner jointly and severally liable for the firm’s tax debt.

issues.definition: If tax was assessed against a partnership as a separate assessment entity and a specific law makes its partners jointly and severally liable, the partners and their property are liable for the firm’s tax debt.

issues.legal_issue: Applying a partner-liability provision to an outstanding firm tax debt is prospective where the provision was in force before the decree and enforcement, even if the debt arose earlier.
material_facts: The tax arrears related to assessment years preceding the amendment that expressly imposed joint and several liability on partners.
The amendment was in force before the decree in the bank’s suit, and the decree remained unexecuted with the tax claim outstanding.
The Court held that the amendment operated from its effective date and that applying it to the outstanding liability did not give it retrospective effect.
issues.conclusion: The partner-liability provision applied prospectively to the outstanding tax claim; applying it in these circumstances was not retrospective.
issues.legal_principle: Retrospectivity is not inferred unless it is expressed or necessarily implied, particularly where substantive rights and obligations are concerned. An amendment is not retrospective merely because it applies to persons or circumstances covered by the earlier law, if it operates from its effective date rather than an anterior date. The Court relied on the stated principles in Justice G.P. Singh’s Principles of Statutory Interpretation.

predicates.appeal_concerning_enforcement_of_outstan: A party appealed in a dispute over enforcing a firm’s outstanding tax debt against its partners or their property.
predicates.earlier_tax_debt_remains_unpaid: The tax debt arose before the later liability rule but remained outstanding when enforcement was considered.
predicates.later_liability_rule_in_force_before_dec: The rule imposing partner liability was in force before the decree and the enforcement of the outstanding claim.

issues.definition: Where an earlier firm tax debt remains unpaid and a later partner-liability rule is in force before decree and enforcement, the rule applies to that debt prospectively.
